text: A Conditional Access policy that correctly blocks legacy authentication protocols is doing exactly what it was designed to do. If it also blocks a scanner-to-email workflow a warehouse team has used for six years, technically correct won't save it — someone with enough authority demands a same-day rollback, and once a control gets reverted under pressure, it's much harder to bring back. The control passed every test from Lesson 26; it just never survived contact with a real business process nobody mapped first.

Every rollout needs a documented exception path: a specific group, a specific request process, a specific person who can approve a time-limited exclusion for a workflow the policy didn't anticipate. Here, the warehouse team's scanner service account gets added to a logged, time-boxed exception group instead of the policy itself being switched off. Without that path, the only lever anyone has is disabling the whole control — which undermines it for everyone, not just the one team with a problem.

The cheapest risk reduction happens before the change lands at all: telling affected teams and the help desk what's changing, when, and who to contact if something breaks. A help desk that already expects Tuesday's Conditional Access change handles the first failure calmly with a ticket queue ready. A help desk blindsided by that same failure escalates it as an outage — and an outage is exactly what gets a control reverted fast, correct or not.

Lesson 26's pilot group doesn't jump straight to everyone. Enforcement expands in planned waves — a second, larger group, then a third, then the remainder — with time between waves to catch whatever the first pilot missed. Each wave carries a smaller blast radius than jumping straight to full rollout, and each one gives the exception process a chance to work before the next group hits the same issue.

Surviving the rollout still doesn't tell you whether the control actually made the organization safer. Next: measuring risk reduction directly, with a real before-and-after baseline, instead of assuming a deployed control is automatically a working one.
